title: Olympian Says He Just Touched the Water — Now He’s in Court!
summary:
What if touching water could get you in big trouble? That’s what former U.S. Olympian David Hearn is finding out! The 67-year-old canoeist, who competed in three Olympic Games, walked into a Washington, D.C. courtroom on Thursday and pleaded not guilty to damaging the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

Here’s the story: Last month, the pool had just finished a $14 million renovation ordered by the Trump administration. But soon after, the paint started peeling and algae grew in the water. Many people called the remodel a huge failure. Hearn says he was just curious and touched the water. But federal prosecutors say he deliberately damaged the pool and caused more than $1,000 in harm.

Outside the courthouse, a crowd of supporters cheered “Davey! Davey!” One protester, Melanie Davis, said she doesn’t even know Hearn but came because she thinks the case is unfair. “Any one of us could have been Davey Hearn,” she said. “I could have easily walked past that reflecting pool, seen a bit of paint, decided to touch it. And I would have been in this courtroom today.”

Hearn’s lawyers argue the government’s evidence is weak and that he’s being used as a scapegoat — someone blamed for other people’s mistakes. The judge released Hearn without bail, and his next hearing is on August 5. Will touching water really be a crime? We’ll find out!
why_it_matters: This story shows that even a simple action near a famous monument can lead to big legal trouble, reminding kids to be careful around public property where rules are taken very seriously.

background_read: The Lincoln Memorial is a famous monument in Washington, D.C., built to honor President Abraham Lincoln. The Reflecting Pool is a long, shallow pool in front of it that creates a mirror image of the memorial.

The Trump administration (the U.S. government under President Donald Trump) ordered a $14 million renovation of the pool, but the new paint soon peeled and algae grew, leading many people to say the project was a failure.
Sometimes courts must decide if something that seems small—like touching water—is actually a crime when it involves national monuments.
